summary: Redwood led a technical migration/demonstration workshop for LumenGrid focusing on an adapter-style approach to port endpoints from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to the Redwood API. The call covered API parity mapping, Console/Optimize features for batching and quantization, security constraints (VPC/KMS/SOC2), and a preliminary canary plan. Action items were assigned and a follow-up pilot session was tentatively scheduled.
topics: Field-to-field parity mapping (params, stop sequences, streaming, function calls)
Console demo: model selection, rollouts, observability
Optimize: batching, KV cache, quantization recommendations
Security & private deployment concerns (KMS, VPC, audit logs)
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-02-28 14:00 UTC | Duration 72 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Taylor Chen (LumenGrid CTO), Ivy Morales (Lead ML Eng), Ravi Singh (PM)

[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Taylor (CTO): Hi, Taylor here.
[00:09] Ivy: Ivy on my side.
[00:11] Ravi: Ravi here.
[00:13] Samir (SE): Samir from Redwood, hello.
[00:15] Alex: Awesome. Goal for today — run through an adapter pattern for porting your OpenAI/Anthropic/Together endpoints to Redwood API, show Console and Optimize levers, and surface any tricky parity issues. We'll leave time for questions and next steps.

[02:05] Alex: Quick context question — what's your primary latency target and current throughput?
[02:12] Taylor: We're targeting p95 220-250ms for short prompts, although for some doc summarization flows p95 can be 800ms to 1.2s. Throughput: peak around 40 rps for chat endpoint, avg 12 rps.
[02:30] Ivy: Also want to note we use a mixture of GPT-like chat completions and Together-style seq2seq with function-style outputs; we do post-processing and reranking on our side.

[04:00] Samir: Good, that helps. Adapter pattern we recommend is kind of a thin shim service that translates param names and handles tokenization differences, stop sequences, and function call schemas before calling Redwood. This keeps your product code unchanged while we validate parity.
[04:26] Ravi: So basically a translation layer? Are there gotchas around streaming and partial tokens?

[04:40] Samir: Yes. Streaming behaviors vary: OpenAI streams chunk deltas, Anthropic may stream in a slightly different framing, and Together's SDK has its own chunk format. Redwood supports server-sent events and websocket streaming; we can map chunks to your current format in the shim. A common issue is token boundary handling — you might see a partial token split differently, so the shim should coalesce pieces until a token boundary if your client expects that.

[07:10] Ivy: Tokenization differences — we saw a few edge cases where our existing tokenizer splits emojis and CJK differently. Will Redwood's token counts materially change cost math?
[07:25] Samir: We have tokenizers aligned to most open models shipped in the catalog, but bytes-level diffs can occur. Our Optimize tool can run a small sample of your prompts to estimate token delta; we'll put that in the parity spreadsheet. Expect small variance, usually within +-5-7% for most English short prompts, but could be higher for emojis or rare languages.

[09:02] Alex: Demo time — I'll share my screen and flip to the Console.
[09:10] [screen share] Alex: Here's the models catalog. For your use case I'd recommend testing 'redwood-llm-large-v2' and a quantized variant for Dedicated. You can pin versions, create a rollout, or set fallback policies.
[10:00] Alex: Watch the Route config — you can set per-route defaults for temperature, max_tokens, stop sequences, streaming true/false, and model families. That maps cleanly to the adapter props.

[11:30] Taylor: How do you handle function/tool calling? Our production code relies heavily on structured function outputs.
[11:38] Samir: Redwood supports function calling with structured JSON output; we also support enforced schemas and post-validation hooks in the runtime. The adapter can remap Together/OpenAI function call schemas to Redwood's shape. One caveat: if you rely on exact ordering or extra metadata, include that in the shim translation.

[13:55] Ivy: Any differences in stop sequence semantics? We've got a few custom delimiter cases.
[14:05] Samir: Good question. Stop sequence matching can be different: some runtimes do substring stopping, others token-level. Redwood exposes stop sequence mode and has a 'hard stop' option in the Route config. We'll document help notes in the parity doc.

[15:40] Alex: Now Optimize — this is where we reduce unit cost. Samir, walk through batching and KV cache.
[15:48] Samir: Sure. Two levers: continuous batching at the runtime layer, and KV cache for prefix reuse. For your reranking flow, batching at a 25-100ms window can greatly increase throughput without harming p95 too much. KV cache helps when you have repeated system prompts or long context prefixes — we saw up to 30% token cost drop in a similar use case.
[17:10] Ravi: How about quantization impact on quality? We can't accept hallucination increases.
[17:18] Samir: We'll run a small eval with your prompts. Our Optimize recommendations include quantization profiles (8-bit, 4-bit mixed) with measured perplexity and alignment on your eval set. If you need absolute parity we recommend starting on an FP16 variant for functional parity, then try quantized profiles and monitor quality regressions via the Console evals.

[19:33] Ivy: Can we run canary traffic to Redwood Hosted first before moving to Dedicated?
[19:40] Alex: Yes, our smart routing lets you route e.g., 5% to Redwood Hosted and 95% to your current provider, or route by customer tier. Also we support a private control plane if you want a VPC or on-prem package for data residency.

[21:50] Taylor: Security — SSO, KMS, audit logs, and SOC2 — what's the path for us?
[21:58] Samir: Redwood has SOC2 Type II, SAML/SSO integrations, RBAC, and audit logs. For key management we support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM and integrate with common cloud KMS providers. For Private deployments we can do customer-controlled VPCs; audit logs land in your storage or our secure retention depending on the plan. We'll send the security pack.

[24:30] Ivy: A quick nit — how do we reproduce Together's prompt-engineered system roles? They use a layered system where sometimes system role is prepended, sometimes injected mid-turn.
[24:45] Samir: The adapter can normalize role tokens. We also support role-specific prefix caching so you can pre-cache repeated system tokens separate from user messages. That reduces repeated encoding cost.

[27:00] Alex: Now I'll show a quick parity spreadsheet template — Samir, can you pull that?
[27:08] Samir: Yup. [screen shows spreadsheet] Columns: source provider, endpoint, param map (temperature -> temperature), streaming semantics, function call mapping, token delta estimate, test prompt id, expected p95, notes. We'll populate with your sample prompts.

[29:22] Taylor: For our embed endpoints, cost is a big driver. Does Redwood have an embeddings endpoint equivalent?
[29:30] Samir: Yes, we have embeddings with per-vector pricing, and Optimize can suggest quantized vector encodings and caching for frequently-requested vectors. If you have heavy similarity search we can suggest an L2/ann strategy and cache.

[31:55] Ivy: Any telemetry hooks? We want token-level cost breakdown per route.
[32:02] Alex: Console has token-level breakdowns, per-route cost windows, per-token latency histograms, and we expose tracing hooks to pipe into your observability stack. You can also export raw traces for a month or longer if needed.

[34:10] Ravi: A painful area: legal/procurement — we need data deletion assurances and contractual language for PII. Who handles that?
[34:21] Samir: That goes through our sales/legal SOW process. For Hosted we have retention and deletion terms; for Dedicated/Private you can keep data entirely on customer-managed infra. We'll loop in Solutions Engineering + Legal; Alex will drive the contract ask.

[36:50] Alex: Let's demo a quick API call from the Console test playground to show parity. I'm going to send a small chat request and enable streaming.
[36:58] [typing sounds]
[37:12] Alex: Note the response comes as SSE events; here's the chunk framing. If your client expects Together framing we'll wrap that in the shim so no change to front-end.

[39:30] Ivy: Seeing a small difference in token counts here — some multi-byte chars counted differently. We'll send samples.
[39:38] Samir: Please do, Ivy. Put them in the shared folder and I'll add token-delta columns in the spreadsheet.

[41:05] Taylor: Can you explain how rollouts work — we want to A/B model families and have automatic fallback to cheaper quantized variant if latency spikes.
[41:15] Samir: You can create a rollout policy with weights, and set a fallback rule: if p95 > threshold or error rate > x% then route to fallback model. Policies can be per-tenant or global, and we log decisions for audit.

[43:50] Ravi: Thoughts on Dedicated sizing — we run bursts especially during day-end processing windows.
[43:58] Samir: For predictable bursts we suggest a baseline reserved capacity with burst pool. We'll propose node counts and GPU types in the sizing doc. Also autoscaling triggers can be tied to queue latency or queue size.

[46:30] Ivy: For the KV cache — is it sharded or per-machine? We have multi-region needs.
[46:38] Samir: KV cache is sharded by model+prefix key and can be regionalized. For multi-region low-latency we recommend colocated caches with cross-region invalidation policies. We'll include recommended TTLs based on your access patterns.

[49:10] Alex: Quick live Q&A — open to anything.
[49:15] Taylor: What's the typical time to do a proof-of-concept? We want measurable parity and cost delta in two weeks if possible.
[49:23] Samir: Typical POC is 2-4 weeks. If you provide prompts, sample logs, and a few endpoints to map, we can do an initial hosted canary in 10-14 days.

[51:00] Ivy: Any gotchas with stream resumption or reconnects? We need to support mobile clients with flaky networks.
[51:06] Samir: Redwood stream client supports resumption tokens; if the client disconnects we can resume from the last confirmed token. That said, partial token boundary handling is important in the shim.

[53:10] Ravi: Are there specific SDKs for our stack? We're mostly Node + Go.
[53:15] Alex: We have official SDKs for Node, Python, Go and a straightforward HTTP REST interface. The shim can be a tiny Node service with our SDK for simplicity.

[55:45] Ivy: We need a runbook for cutover in case something breaks in production. Can Redwood provide one?
[55:53] Samir: Yes, we'll include a cutover checklist: feature flag route, 1%/5%/25% ramps, fallback rules, monitoring dashboards to watch, and rollback steps.

[58:30] Taylor: Ok, recap and next steps?
[58:36] Alex: Recap: we'll deliver the parity spreadsheet template, run a token-delta sample on your provided prompts, propose Dedicated sizing + pricing, and outline the POC plan. Samir will own the parity doc, Alex will run pricing and contract touchpoints.

[59:05] Taylor: Sounds good. Tentative dates?
[59:10] Alex: I put target dates in the next steps — share by 2026-03-03 for the mapping doc, pricing by 2026-03-02, and then plan a canary planning on 2026-03-10.

[60:00] Ivy: Slight note — some of our prompts include inline XML and tables that trip tokenizers. We'll send examples to the shared drive.
[60:10] Samir: Great — please add a couple dozen prompts across common patterns, rarer languages, and the XML cases. We'll prioritize those in eval.

[64:20] Ravi: Two quick procurement questions: do you have a standard MSA template and do you support PO terms?
[64:28] Alex: Yes on both; procurement can review MSA and we accept PO terms for enterprise contracts. I'll loop in our sales ops.

[67:00] Taylor: Thanks everyone. That was helpful.
[67:05] Alex: Thanks, we'll follow up with the docs and schedule.
[67:12] Ivy: Thanks.
[67:14] Samir: Thanks all.

[72:00] Call ended.
